analyses.saying: Most commenters call the two-axis framework a workable starting point but not a complete risk determination, asking FDA to account for reversibility, error detectability, time to harm, traceability, autonomy or clinical agency, and patient vulnerability. Many add that human oversight and downstream safeguards should lower risk only with proof they work; several say "incorrect output" omits harms of omission.

disagreement.text: Commenters split on structure: some want the two axes kept as the primary heuristic with reversibility, safeguards, time pressure and traceability operationalized as auditable modifiers, while others want the framework expanded into additional axes or a fuller multi-dimensional set of risk factors.

sides.summary: Keep two axes; treat added factors as modifiers on the existing framework.
Expand to additional axes or a multi-dimensional risk representation.

analyses.saying: Commenters accept directiveness as a continuum and say it should be judged by what an output functionally does, specificity, personalization, urgency, imperative force, omitted alternatives, confidence presentation, not by interface labels or disclaimers. Many ask that it be measured across multi-turn conversational trajectories, and several want anchored rubrics, worked examples, or decision trees for predictability.

disagreement.text: Most commenters want directiveness operationalized through new anchored levels, rubrics, or authority tiers; one argues against any new taxonomy, saying contested new terms would confuse manufacturers and directiveness should instead modify the existing benefit-risk factor of probability of harm.

sides.summary: Create explicit graded scales, anchored rubric levels, five-level authority tiers, or decision trees, with worked examples.
Avoid a new taxonomy; treat directiveness as a modifier within the existing benefit-risk probability-of-harm factor.

analyses.saying: Most commenters accept that patient-facing delivery bears on risk but ask FDA not to treat it as automatically higher risk, tying risk instead to clinical consequence, the user's realistic verification path, and enforceable safeguards. They reject disclaimers as mitigation and would credit only tested features: traceable sourcing, calibrated uncertainty, escalation triggers, and comprehension testing in the actual user population.

disagreement.text: Commenters split on whether patient-facing status itself should raise the risk tier: most say no automatic uplift, with risk set by consequence, context, and demonstrated safeguards; a few say patient-facing or action-directing outputs are higher risk by default because patients cannot contextualize or override them.

sides.summary: Patient-facing delivery is a modifier, not an automatic higher-risk designation; risk turns on consequence, verification path, and verified safeguards.
Patient-facing or action-directing outputs should be treated as higher risk because patients lack training to interpret or override them.

analyses.saying: Most commenters accept that specialist-versus-generalist use bears on risk but reject professional title as the test, urging risk turn on the gap between a function's knowledge domain and the intended user's ability to independently review outputs, validated through error-detection and escalation testing with the least specialized intended user. Cara AI adds a supervised non-clinical worker tier.

disagreement.text: Commenters split on whether user scope can be handled in labeling: some want the intended user's competency level stated in labeling and validated in that population, while others call labeling unenforceable and would credit only technically enforced access controls or workflow-embedded specialist review, assessing risk against foreseeable use.

sides.summary: Specify and validate intended user competency through labeling and intended-use statements.
Labeling cannot enforce user scope; credit only demonstrated technical controls or workflow embedding and judge risk against foreseeable off-label users.

analyses.saying: Nearly all commenters said the whole conversation or session, not the individual turn, should be the unit of risk assessment, and asked FDA to require adversarial multi-turn trajectory testing (escalation, user pressure, long context, session boundaries).

disagreement.text: No material conflict: commenters converge on trajectory-level assessment. What they debate is how to operationalize it, how intended use should be written (conversational scope, directiveness ceiling, permitted trajectories), whether to classify by the highest plausible-risk turn, and what acceptance criteria or bounded escape rates should apply.

analyses.saying: Most commenters ask FDA to require under- and over-escalation to be reported and gated as separate error classes, not blended into one accuracy or utility score, with sponsors prespecifying context- and capacity-justified asymmetric acceptance criteria (for example minimum sensitivity plus maximum over-escalation rate) that FDA reviews.

disagreement.text: Commenters split on which error direction should carry more weight: some say under-escalation is the more severe error and high sensitivity should be permitted or favored, while another argues over-escalation is more dangerous because it causes errors of commission such as unnecessary treatment and testing.

sides.summary: Under-escalation should be treated as the more severe error, allowing sponsors to prioritize sensitivity.
Over-escalation deserves equal or greater weight, given commission harms and diffuse, under-detected system harms.

analyses.saying: Most commenters accept benchmarking followed by clinical confirmation, but attach conditions: assess the final configured device as deployed rather than the underlying foundation model, bind results to an identified configuration, and avoid treating benchmark scores as a surrogate for real clinical performance in higher-risk uses. Several ask FDA to publish how evidence scales with risk.

disagreement.text: Commenters split on whether the clinician-competency analogy can support less testing: some say it justifies only the shape and not the quantity of evidence, and should not replace clinical utility evidence for consequential uses, while others endorse it as-is, including confirming clinically without a prospective study as least-burdensome.

sides.summary: Competency framing must not reduce the amount of evidence; benchmark performance is a surrogate that cannot stand in for real clinical performance in high-risk uses.
The competency-based model and its credentialing analogy are appropriate as described, including flexibility to confirm clinically without a prospective trial.

analyses.saying: Most commenters accept scaling premarket evidence to a function's two-axis risk position, but say the framework is unusable until CDRH publishes an explicit risk-tier-to-evidence mapping specifying minimum benchmarking, confirmation tier, third-party involvement and postmarket monitoring; Walnut Hill Medical also wants tiers tied to 510(k)/De Novo/PMA. Several ask to add dimensions such as autonomy and irreversibility.

disagreement.text: Commenters split over who sets the confirmation level: some say FDA's risk mapping should determine the required approach because sponsor selection with justification invites weaker evidence and inconsistent review, while others keep the sponsor-justified menu and ask only for default tiers or decision criteria.

sides.summary: FDA's risk mapping should dictate the required confirmation approach, not sponsor choice.
Keep sponsor selection and justification, with published default tiers or decision criteria keyed to risk.

analyses.saying: Most commenters call FDA's benchmarking structure a sound starting point but incomplete, and ask for added elements: adversarial input and cybersecurity testing, human factors, citation and provenance fidelity, multi-turn and edge-of-scope behavior, and external-dependency or degraded-mode performance. Many also object to aggregate or pooled scores, asking for subgroup- and failure-mode-level reporting with separate acceptance criteria for safety-critical failures.

disagreement.text: No commenter contradicts another on the substance; positions are additive. The debate is over how far benchmarking scope should extend (foreseeable use, retrieval and orchestration layers, cybersecurity, system dependencies) and how granular acceptance criteria and reporting must be rather than averaged.

analyses.saying: Most commenters say benchmark scores alone cannot establish real-world safety: sponsors should document per-benchmark construct validity tied to intended use, run contamination checks, use sequestered or independently held test sets, and pair benchmarking with clinical confirmation. Sponsor-developed benchmarks are accepted for novel uses, but only with locked thresholds, escrow, or independent adjudication.

disagreement.text: No material conflict appears. Commenters are working out who should hold and maintain sequestered test assets (FDA or a NIST-linked steward, another independent party, or an escrowed sponsor set) and how much construct-validity and contamination evidence sponsors must file before a benchmark can gate evaluation.

analyses.saying: Most commenters accept a graduated ladder of clinical confirmation and agree prospective studies need not always be required, but ask FDA to specify how the tier is chosen rather than leaving it to sponsor justification. Common additions: shadow deployment for intermediate risk, characterization of the anticipated real-world input distribution, subgroup and setting reporting, and evaluation of the deployed human-AI team.

disagreement.text: Commenters split on structure: some want a fixed, ordered ladder with the required tier set by risk classification (or set by FDA rather than sponsor choice), while others want the methods treated as alternative or combinable options chosen by residual uncertainty. One commenter separately opposes any waiver of prospective trials.

sides.summary: Prescribe an ordered, risk-keyed ladder with the required tier determined by FDA's risk mapping.
Treat confirmation methods as complementary or combinable options selected by residual evidentiary uncertainty, not a fixed hierarchy.

analyses.saying: Most commenters told FDA to keep synthetic and real-world results separate, and to pool benchmarking with clinical confirmation only if sampling frames are shown exchangeable, with confirmation governing acceptance. They also asked for disaggregated subgroup, scenario and failure-mode reporting instead of single pooled scores, prespecified estimands and precision, and repeated-run variance reporting to handle nondeterministic outputs.

disagreement.text: Commenters split on whether synthetic data may ever contribute to a performance estimate: some would permit combining after documented transportability, weighting and provenance, while others say synthetic data provides no valid denominator, no validated adequacy method exists, and it should be limited to failure-finding and rare-event coverage.

sides.summary: Combining synthetic and real evidence is acceptable when transportability, provenance and distributional differences are documented.
Synthetic data must never establish performance rates; it lacks a real-population denominator and no validated adequacy method exists.

analyses.saying: Commenters accept synthetic data only as a supplement, for rare events, adversarial and stress testing, controlled perturbations, and privacy-limited coverage, and not for establishing performance rates, subgroup claims, or benefit-risk conclusions. Most ask FDA to guard against correlated blind spots through generator lineage disclosure and separation, independent or multiple generators, real-world holdouts, and separate real/synthetic reporting.

disagreement.text: Commenters split on whether synthetic-to-real adequacy can be demonstrated: some would allow pooled or supplemental use if generators are independently validated against real distributions and transportability or distributional shift is analyzed, while others say no validated method exists for showing distributional adequacy and FDA should assume none does.

sides.summary: Synthetic data can supplement or be pooled if generators are independently validated against real distributions and shift/transportability is documented.
No validated method exists to show a synthetic population is distributionally adequate to a real one; FDA should presume none and bar synthetic data from performance-rate and subgroup claims.

analyses.saying: Commenters ask that comparators be anchored to the device's labeled intended user and the care patients would otherwise receive, with acceptance criteria prespecified from the consequence of an incorrect output. Several reject the "median clinician in practice" bar; clinician panels are validated, blinded adjudication instruments with reported inter-rater reliability, and team performance is primary where labeling requires human review.

disagreement.text: Commenters split over benchmarking against actual practice. Some want performance judged against the care available without the device, including delayed or no intervention; others say prevailing or median practice normalizes existing variation and want an evidence-based standard or an absolute safety floor for high-risk functions.

sides.summary: Compare the device to the care patients would actually receive absent it, including no or delayed intervention.
Reject median or prevailing practice as the bar; require an evidence-based clinical standard or absolute safety floor.

analyses.saying: Most commenters accept assessing performance against the care patients would otherwise receive, including unaided judgment, delayed specialist review, or no intervention, but ask that the counterfactual be prespecified, empirically demonstrated for the deployment setting, and carried into labeling, with device-alone and human-AI performance reported separately. Several would pair it with an absolute safety floor.

disagreement.text: Commenters split on whether the real-world counterfactual can stand alone. Some say holding access-expanding or low-risk tools to a standard the delivery system does not meet protects no one; others say a current-practice baseline entrenches substandard care and must be paired with an absolute safety floor or evidence-based standard.

sides.summary: Actual prevailing care, including no intervention, is a legitimate primary comparator, especially for access-expanding uses.
Counterfactual comparison alone risks normalizing weak baselines; require an absolute safety floor or an evidence-based standard alongside it.

analyses.saying: Most commenters back a limited third-party role in the tasks where independence is the point, custody of sequestered test sets, benchmark administration, adversarial testing, and clinical adjudication, conditioned on published qualification and conflict-of-interest criteria, multiple accredited providers (often modeled on ASCA/MDDT), and retained sponsor accountability and FDA decision authority. Several note third-party assessment capacity does not yet exist at scale.

disagreement.text: Commenters split on whether third-party review should be required. Some would mandate independent premarket testing and recurring audits for high-impact systems; others accept it only as an optional pathway with a preserved first-party route, and one commenter opposes any requirement, arguing third parties could prolong testing for profit.

sides.summary: Independent premarket testing and recurring audits should be required, at least for high-impact systems; manufacturer self-assessment alone is not enough.
Third-party involvement should be optional or is inadvisable as a requirement, keeping a first-party route available.

analyses.saying: Nearly all commenters accept extending the competency-based approach to multimodal, world-model and other architectures, but ask that evaluation target the final configured device's behavior and function rather than its technical design, adding failure modes such as cross-modal consistency, error propagation and agentic authority. Two note benchmarks are thinner here and want clinical confirmation weighted more heavily.

disagreement.text: Commenters split on whether requirements should be architecture-neutral. Most want criteria anchored in intended function and device behavior, warning architecture-specific rules go stale; a few want the underlying architecture assessed in every case, with architecture-specific tests and higher risk categorization for vision-language models.

sides.summary: Keep evaluation architecture-agnostic, focused on the configured device's function, inputs/outputs and downstream authority.
Require architecture-specific assessment, tests and risk categorization tied to the underlying model type and modality.

analyses.saying: Most commenters accept trading premarket evidence for postmarket monitoring only under stated conditions: prespecified, enforceable monitoring plans with triggers and thresholds, demonstrated detection speed and coverage, reversible harm, and rollback authority. Many would bar the trade for high-consequence, autonomous, or poorly observable functions. Several question whether monitoring reliably detects novel or unreported failures at all.

disagreement.text: Most commenters would bound the trade with explicit conditions and carve-outs for high-consequence, irreversible, or autonomous functions, and some reject it outright as unsuited to a new technology; a minority urges broad latitude, with market forces as the main constraint and a rule that requirements not exceed those on existing care.

sides.summary: Allow generative AI wide latitude; regulatory requirements should not exceed the human standard of care being replaced.
Permit reduced premarket evidence only under enforceable, verified monitoring conditions, or not at all for high-consequence and autonomous functions.

analyses.saying: Most commenters accept periodic re-benchmarking, sample-based clinician review, and degradation monitoring as complementary but too narrow, urging monitoring of overrides, near misses, subgroup and workflow effects, human-AI team performance, and clinical outcomes. Many ask that reassessment be event-triggered (model, prompt, retrieval, population, or safety-signal changes) alongside a calendar floor, and that version and configuration records be reconstructable.

disagreement.text: Commenters split on cadence: some would drop fixed intervals and re-benchmark only on defined events, while others want a default risk-tiered periodic schedule (quarterly to annual) or an annual calendar floor with out-of-cycle triggers layered on top.

sides.summary: Reassessment should be event- or trigger-driven rather than on a fixed periodic schedule.
Keep a scheduled baseline cadence set by risk (or an annual floor), with event triggers added.

analyses.saying: Commenters accept machine-based supervisory agents as an aid to postmarket monitoring only if the supervisor is validated and independently evaluated, measured detection sensitivity and false-flag rates, version control, audit logs, and re-evaluation over time. The most repeated condition is independence from the monitored device to avoid correlated failure when both share a foundation model, with human adjudication retained for final judgments.

disagreement.text: No commenter opposes another's substantive position. The debate is over how much authority a supervisory agent may hold (triage and flagging versus terminal decisions), how independence from the monitored model should be demonstrated, and what validation and change-control treatment the supervisor itself requires.

analyses.saying: Nearly all commenters accept outside contributions to postmarket monitoring only if roles are split by distinct function, with manufacturers keeping the monitoring program, complaint handling, aggregation, and corrective action. Many ask FDA to specify what manufacturers must supply institutions, version identifiers, logs, notice of model changes, and to name omitted actors such as clinical engineering staff, payers, and patients.

disagreement.text: Commenters split on how much monitoring work deploying institutions should do: one says institutions should only inventory functions, retain manufacturer logs, and report failures, not evaluate independently, because capacity varies; others assign institutions local validation, workflow and protocol monitoring, and defined reporting pathways.

sides.summary: Institutional role should be limited to inventory, log retention, and reporting; evaluation burden belongs with manufacturers.
Institutions should actively monitor locally, including local validation, workflow and protocol changes, and owned reporting pathways.

analyses.saying: Most commenters propose tiered change control keyed to clinical or behavioral impact, not code magnitude: no re-testing where outputs cannot change, quality-system-managed re-benchmarking against a locked baseline suite, and premarket review for model-family or provider swaps, scope expansion, and agentic action changes.

disagreement.text: Commenters split on third-party foundation model changes: some would treat any move to a different model family or provider-forced migration as the highest tier requiring premarket review, while others would let like-for-like model version upgrades be handled under a PCCP with prespecified re-benchmarking inside the quality system.

sides.summary: Model-family or provider-initiated model changes belong in the highest tier, with premarket submission and independent revalidation, regardless of whether the change was involuntary.
Model version upgrades and drift should be manageable under flexible PCCPs and the sponsor's quality system with prespecified re-benchmarking, avoiding repeated supplemental submissions.

analyses.saying: Most commenters said prespecifying every future modification is unworkable for generative systems and asked FDA to reframe PCCPs around limits that must hold: locked benchmarks and acceptance thresholds, deviation bounds, monitoring, rollback, and triggers for a new submission. Many also asked for tiered change categories and specific provisions for third-party foundation model updates.

disagreement.text: Commenters split on how much change can be handled inside the sponsor's quality system: some want every material change independently verified before deployment, while others want tiers permitting documentation-only or quality-system-managed changes, including like-for-like model version upgrades, without new submissions.

sides.summary: Every material change should be independently revalidated or verified before release.
Lower tiers should allow documentation-only or quality-system-managed changes, including like-for-like model upgrades, without repeat submissions.

analyses.saying: Commenters overwhelmingly ask FDA to spell out concrete dependency controls: pinning to a version-identified model endpoint, contractual advance change notice and deprecation windows, technical detection through fingerprints, canary and shadow testing, regression re-benchmarking, quarantine and rollback, with the manufacturer accountable for device behavior when upstream models change. Several would tier such changes within a PCCP.

disagreement.text: Commenters split on how binding pinning and notice should be: some would make a pinned, version-identified endpoint with contractual change notice a design-control expectation whose absence is a design deficiency, while others frame pinning or equivalent controls as applying where technically and contractually feasible, seeking sufficient information rather than full visibility or control.

sides.summary: Pinning and advance change notice should be mandatory expectations, with absence treated as a design deficiency or higher evidence burden.
Pinning or equivalent change-detection controls should apply where feasible; the goal is enough information and device-level controls to detect and respond, not full control of the model.

analyses.saying: Nearly all commenters accept the master file concept but say voluntary disclosure alone won't close gaps, asking FDA to specify minimum, versioned content, training-data cutoff, model identity and version lineage, known failure modes, subgroup evaluations, change and deprecation notification, keeping the deployed device the unit of evaluation, with sponsors holding contractual information rights. Supernova Technologies questions self-filed disclosures entirely.

disagreement.text: Commenters split on how to fix weak developer incentives: some would keep the program voluntary and confidential while shifting evidence burden or creating procurement pressure when no master file exists, while others want required disclosure, contractual disclosure duties, or a public subset of master file content.

sides.summary: Keep participation voluntary and proprietary content protected; drive disclosure through incentives, burden-shifting defaults, or a narrow public tier evaluated before any requirement.

Voluntary disclosure is inadequate; FDA should expect or require foundation-model information, mandate minimum content, add contractual duties and authority to request more, or expose a public subset.

analyses.saying: Nearly all commenters say agentic devices need evaluation beyond output quality: acceptance criteria applied to complete action trajectories rather than per-step accuracy, enumerated action inventories classified by reversibility, least-privilege tool permissions, confirmation before irreversible actions, audit logs allowing full reconstruction, rollback and safe-state reversion, and prompt-injection testing, with criteria tightening as autonomy rises and human review declines.

disagreement.text: Commenters split on whether autonomous execution can ever be authorized: some propose staged or graduated authorization letting devices operate unsupervised once predefined competency and real-world thresholds are met, while others would require a named clinician's pre-action approval for every consequential or irreversible action, keeping AI in an informing role.

sides.summary: Autonomy can expand after demonstrated competence, via staged or graduated authorization tied to performance thresholds.
Human authorization must precede every consequential or irreversible action, with AI limited to informing.
